Tight
TITE
adjective (Silent Generation slang)
From Middle English thight, dense, close-packed, from a Scandinavian root; the 1828 senses are close, compact, firmly held. American slang has borrowed the word more than once (it meant drunk by the 1830s, a separate sense); the sense "close, intimate," of friends — "those two are tight" — is recorded by the mid-twentieth century and was at home in 1950s talk. The picture is of a knot pulled so tight it will not slip.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

When a boy of 1955 said he and his buddy were tight, he meant they were close as two fingers — they rode bikes together, sat together at the ballgame, and would stand up for each other in the schoolyard. That is one of the oldest good things in the world, and Scripture tells its finest story. After David killed Goliath, "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1Sa 18:1). That was tight: a king’s son who risked his father’s anger to protect his friend. Proverbs puts it plainly: "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Pro 17:17). It also warns that the friends we are tight with will shape us: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Pro 13:20). The best of it is that the Lord Jesus calls His people into that same closeness: "Henceforth I call you not servants… but I have called you friends" (Joh 15:15). He is the "friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24), and He proved it by laying down His life for His friends. A grandfather can tell a grandchild: be tight with good friends, and be tightest of all with Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (1950s) for close, intimate, of friends ("those two are tight") — from the 1828 sense of close and firmly held, and a picture of the friend that sticketh closer than a brother (Pro 18:24).

expand to see more

TIGHT, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) Close in friendship; inseparable. "Jimmy and Bob are tight — you never see one without the other."

Webster (1828) — TIGHT, adjective 1. Close; compact; not loose or open; having the joints so close that no fluid can enter or escape; not leaky; as a tight ship, or a tight cask. 3. Sitting close to the body; as a tight coat or other garment. 6. Close; parsimonious; saving; as a man tight in his dealings. [In common use in America.]

Decode for families: "we’re tight" means "we’re close friends" — not stingy, and not anything worse.

Key Scripture

1Sa 18:1 — "And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul."

Pro 17:17 — "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity."

Pro 18:24 — "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother."

Pro 13:20 — "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed."

Joh 15:15 — "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you."

Modern Corruption

A good word for a good thing; the only caution is that a tight circle can harden into a clique that shuts others out, or bind a young person to the wrong crowd.

expand to see more

There is nothing to correct in tight as a word for friendship. Close friends are a gift of God, and the Bible honours them. The word does have an older slang cousin that is not so wholesome — tight once meant drunk — and families should know the difference, but the 1950s sense is clean.

The cautions are two. A tight group can become a closed one, where outsiders are mocked and newcomers frozen out; Christ’s friendship is the opposite of a clique, for He received sinners and ate with them. And being tight with fools is dangerous, however warm it feels (Pro 13:20). Teach children to choose friends who will make them wiser, and then to be the kind of friend Jonathan was.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Scandinavian root (dense) → Middle English thight → English tight (close, firm) → mid-20th c. slang (close friends).
